title: When the climb stops ending: cell death, senescence, and cancer

objectives.statement: Calculate, from a crypt's cell count and its renewal interval, how many cells one crypt must lose per day, state the condition that keeps its cell number steady, and use that rate relation to show how small a sustained mismatch between production and loss has to be in order to change the tissue.

Distinguish apoptosis from accidental cell death by what happens to the dying cell's contents and to the tissue around it, explain why that difference matters to an epithelium one cell thick, and explain why a necrotic appearance does not by itself establish whether a dedicated pathway was running.

Explain attachment to the basement membrane as a survival condition for an epithelial cell, predict the consequence for a tissue of a cell that survives detachment, and separate what the evidence on shedding and extrusion establishes from what it leaves unsettled, including the order of death and detachment.

Distinguish cellular senescence from apoptosis and from elapsed time, and state both consequences that follow from a cell which stops dividing permanently and stays in the tissue, without resolving the tension between them.

Explain, using evidence that normal functioning tissue carries driver mutations under positive selection, why a driver mutation is not sufficient for cancer; state what that evidence does and does not settle about whether one is necessary; and name what the surrounding tissue contributes to the outcome.

Given a described tissue, identify which controls of the renewal loop appear to be operating, which appear to have failed and which are untested, name every part of the loop where the imbalance could still sit without narrowing it further than the description allows, and state what the description does not license a reader to conclude.

scenes.title: Where a hundred and seventy-five cells a day go
A cell that takes itself apart
Attachment as permission to stay alive
The cells that stop and stay
Working out how badly the loop has to fail
Practice: work the balance, then say what you cannot tell
Clinical wrap-up: reading a growth without diagnosing anyone
